---
title: "Classification"
description: >
  Binary and multiclass outcomes, probabilities and classes, the components on
  the scale of the scores, and the losses.
---

```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 7,
  fig.height = 3.5,
  out.width = "100%"
)
```

For a factor outcome (binary or multi-class with more than two classes), `rpf()` fits a classification model.
It takes the same steps as for regression, with the same defaults: the number of splits is chosen out of bag, the components are pruned, and three-way components are simplified such that each can be shown as the sum of at most 10 heat maps.
The model predicts scores, and every score is a sum of components, as the prediction of a regression model is.
With the losses `"logit"` (the default) and `"exponential"`, the scores are on the log-odds scale: with two classes there is one score, the log-odds of the second class, and with more classes there is one score per class, and the scores sum to 0.
With `"L1"` and `"L2"` the scores are not log-odds but fitted 0/1 class indicators.
The losses are described in "The losses" below.

```{r setup, message = FALSE}
library(randomPlantedForest)
library(glex)
library(ggplot2)

penguins <- na.omit(palmerpenguins::penguins)
```

## Two classes

```{r binary}
set.seed(1)
by_sex <- rpf(sex ~ ., data = penguins, nthreads = 2)
by_sex
```

`predict()` returns probabilities by default, classes with `type = "class"`, and the scores with `type = "link"`:

```{r binary-predict}
predict(by_sex, head(penguins))
predict(by_sex, head(penguins), type = "class")
predict(by_sex, head(penguins), type = "link")
```

## The components, on the scale of the scores

The components add up to the scores, not to the probabilities:

```{r binary-components}
comp <- predict_components(by_sex, penguins)
head(comp$m)
all.equal(comp$intercept + rowSums(comp$m), predict(by_sex, penguins, type = "link")$.pred)
```

With two classes there is one score, the log-odds of the second level of the outcome (here `male`): a positive contribution moves a penguin towards `male`, a negative one towards `female`.
glex draws them as for regression:

```{r binary-plot, fig.alt = "The body mass component of the sex model as a step curve on the scale of the scores."}
autoplot(comp, "body_mass_g")
```

## Three or more classes

With more classes, the model has one score per class, and the scores sum to 0.
The difference of two classes' scores is the log-odds of one class against the other.
Every component has one column per class:

```{r multiclass}
set.seed(1)
by_species <- rpf(species ~ ., data = penguins, nthreads = 2)
by_species
predict(by_species, penguins[c(1, 200, 300), ])
```

```{r multiclass-components}
comp3 <- predict_components(by_species, penguins)
comp3$target_levels
names(comp3$m)[1:6]
comp3$intercept
```

The columns are named `<component>__class:<level>`, one for each of `Adelie`, `Chinstrap` and `Gentoo`.
A positive contribution moves a penguin towards that class, a negative one away from it, and no class is singled out as a reference.
A component is kept or dropped for all classes together: its size is its variance summed over the classes' scores, centred across the classes.
glex draws one panel per score:

```{r multiclass-plot, fig.alt = "The bill length component of the species model, one panel for each class."}
autoplot(comp3, "bill_length_mm")
```

## How the choices are scored

Every out-of-bag choice, of the number of splits and of the pruning, is scored by the loss's own criterion, corrected for the number of out-of-bag families as for regression:

- for the losses that give probabilities, the log-loss of the probabilities `predict(type = "prob")` returns;
- for `loss = "L1"` and `"L2"`, which fit class indicators directly, the squared error of the scores summed over the classes (the Brier score).

## The losses

`loss` chooses how the families fit the classes:

- `"logit"` (the default) and `"exponential"` fit scores on the link scale, and `predict(type = "prob")` returns their softmax, so the probabilities are proper.
  With two classes there is one score, the log-odds of the second class.
  With more, both have one score per class, summing to 0, so the link predictions and the components have one column per class. `"logit"` is the multinomial log-likelihood and `"exponential"` the multiclass exponential loss SAMME.
- `"L1"` and `"L2"` fit 0/1 class indicators directly, as regression would; their scores are not probabilities, and `type = "prob"` truncates them to [0, 1].

### A step, and the pseudo-row

Every split moves the scores of the rows of each of its two new leaves by one step.
For `"exponential"` and `"logit"`, the step minimises the leaf's *penalised* loss: the loss of its rows plus that of one imaginary row, the pseudo-row, split evenly over the classes and placed at the score the leaf has now.
The pseudo-row says "stay where you are", so it pulls every step towards no change, and more so the fewer rows the leaf has.

Two things follow:

- **A pure leaf stops at a finite level.**
  If all rows of a leaf have one class, the loss of its rows alone falls forever as its score grows, and an unpenalised step would push the score to infinity.
  The pseudo-row, which holds a share of the other classes, stops it: with two classes a pure leaf of `n` rows goes to about `log(2n + 1)` and then stays there.
- **A pure split or a repeat gains nothing.**
  A split is scored by what its two leaves' steps gain over the step the parent leaf would make by itself, and each new leaf pays for its own pseudo-row.
  Splitting a pure leaf cannot separate anything, and repeating a split whose leaves are already at their best level cannot improve them, so both score no gain and are not made.
  A round in which no candidate gains makes no split (it still counts towards `n_splits`).

The table shows the score of a point in a pure region as one tree family grows: the two classes are separated by `x1 > 0.5`, and `x2` is noise.

```{r pure-region}
set.seed(1)
n <- 200
sep <- data.frame(x1 = runif(n), x2 = runif(n))
sep$y <- factor(ifelse(sep$x1 > 0.5, "b", "a"))

rounds <- c(5, 10, 30, 100, 300)
score_after <- function(loss, k) {
  set.seed(3)
  f <- rpf(y ~ ., data = sep, loss = loss, n_families = 1, n_splits = k, prune = FALSE)
  c(score = predict(f, data.frame(x1 = 0.9, x2 = 0.5), type = "link")$.pred,
    leaves = nrow(rpf_boxes(f)) - 1)
}
pure <- data.frame(
  rounds = rounds,
  t(sapply(rounds, function(k) score_after("exponential", k))),
  t(sapply(rounds, function(k) score_after("logit", k)))
)
names(pure) <- c("rounds", "exponential score", "exponential leaves", "logit score", "logit leaves")
pure
```

The score stays at its level from the first rounds on, and the family soon stops adding leaves: no candidate gains any more.
So a fixed, large `n_splits` does not make the model overconfident.

### `exact_step`

`"exponential"`'s step has a closed form, so it is exact.
`"logit"` scores the candidates by the second-order (Newton) gain of its penalised loss.
With `exact_step = TRUE` (the default), the chosen split's two leaves then get the exact minimisers, by Newton's method on their rows; `exact_step = FALSE` keeps the one Newton step, which is a little faster.
The search is the same either way, and `exact_step` does not change `"exponential"` fits.
